services.educational_note: File Transfer Protocol transmits credentials in cleartext. It should be replaced with SFTP or FTPS in any production environment.
Secure Shell provides encrypted remote access. Ensure key-based authentication is enforced and password login is disabled.
Telnet sends all data—including passwords—as plaintext. It is considered obsolete and must never be used on any network.
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol is used to send email. Open relays are a common attack vector; always require authentication.
Domain Name System translates hostnames to IPs. Misconfigured DNS servers can expose zone-transfer data or be abused for amplification attacks.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol serves web content without encryption. All production traffic should be redirected to HTTPS (port 443).
Post Office Protocol 3 retrieves email. The unencrypted version on port 110 should be disabled in favour of POP3S on port 995.
Microsoft Remote Procedure Call has historically been exploited (e.g., MS03-026). It should be blocked at the network perimeter.
NetBIOS Session Service exposes Windows name resolution data. It should be disabled externally and replaced with DNS.
Internet Message Access Protocol allows email synchronisation. Use IMAPS (port 993) with TLS to protect credentials in transit.
HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt web traffic. Ensure TLS 1.2+ is enforced, weak cipher suites are disabled, and certificates are valid.
Server Message Block was exploited by EternalBlue (WannaCry). Port 445 must never be exposed to the internet.
MySQL database port. Database servers should only listen on loopback or a dedicated private interface, never on a public IP.
Remote Desktop Protocol is a prime target for brute-force and BlueKeep-style exploits. Restrict it to a VPN or specific IP allowlist.
PostgreSQL database port. Like MySQL, it should never be internet-facing; use a firewall rule or bind only to 127.0.0.1.
Virtual Network Computing provides remote desktop access. Many VNC implementations have weak or no authentication by default.
Redis has no authentication by default and can be used to write files to disk. Never expose it publicly without AUTH and TLS.
Alternate HTTP port commonly used for development servers and proxies. Ensure it is not leaking internal application details.
Alternate HTTPS port. Verify TLS configuration is as rigorous as the primary HTTPS service.
MongoDB's default port has historically been exposed without authentication, leading to mass data breaches. Always require auth and bind to loopback.
SMTP is the core mail-transfer protocol. Ensure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records are configured to prevent email spoofing.
Unencrypted POP3 exposes email credentials. Migrate users to POP3S (995) or IMAP with STARTTLS.
IMAP on port 143 should enforce STARTTLS. Prefer IMAPS (993) for mandatory TLS from connection start.
SMTP over SSL/TLS (implicit TLS). This is the preferred method for mail submission from email clients.
Mail Submission Agent port. Enforce STARTTLS and require SASL authentication on this port.
IMAP over TLS provides encrypted email synchronisation. Verify the TLS certificate and cipher suite configuration.
POP3 over TLS. Acceptable if users prefer POP3, but IMAPS offers more flexibility for multi-device access.
Alternative SMTP port sometimes used when port 25 is blocked by ISPs. Less commonly targeted but should still enforce TLS.
Sieve script management port. If not in use, disable it; if active, require TLS and strong authentication.
SpamAssassin's spamd interface. Bind to loopback only and verify no unauthenticated external access is possible.
